Question: Is it possible for me to double major in civil engineering and psychology, working as a engineer then getting my doctorate and transitioning to a psychiatrist?
Old_Answer: Theoretically, it’s possible. But I would say it’s not close to a rational choice. If you are in the U.S., “psychiatrist” requires getting a MD and doing the appropriate residency. If that’s your goal, you need to get to that goal as quickly as possible. Four years of medical school and four years of residency only gets harder and more expensive as you get older, while your money-making years shrink. Medical school is a full time anti-job (you’re working a full time job and paying as much money as most people wish they were making). If you wanted to be a “psychologist,” that requires a PhD or PsyD. Still many years doing full time study, although you should get paid to do a PhD. If you were trying to accumulate money by being an engineer, civil engineering is the last engineering discipline I would choose. There’s no overlap with the biology and chemistry MD prerequisites and the pay is one of the lowest in engineering. People who are actually committed to civil engineering are busy acquiring the Professional Engineer designation so they can move up in their careers (and make more money). I would focus on a single major/degree and excel. Splitting your attention is probably going to kill your opportunities in both fields. Every PhD I know with a double undergraduate major regretted it in the end, and most double majors don’t make it to a doctorate.

Question: Why is it not easy to get jobs after majoring in bioengineering?
Old_Answer: The jobs aren’t there. In the U.S. and a few other countries, there are more bioengineering undergraduate students than total bioengineering jobs. All jobs, not just entry level ones. Basic supply and demand dictates that most bioengineering students aren’t going to get bioengineering jobs, and the ones that do get jobs are going to be paid less than engineers of similar ability in other fields. It doesn’t take an engineering degree to figure that out. I was alerted to this gross imbalance by one of my former bioengineering professors, who was wondering why his students weren’t finding jobs. You can look up the same numbers via ASEE (graduation count) and BLS (job count). The money imbalance wasn’t as bad as it was several years ago, but the job availability still isn’t there. My wife was biochem + chemical engineering majors and I was an electrical engineering undergraduate. We’re not letting our kids major in bioengineering: they’re better off being in the area which has bioengineering applications, so they have options. EE, ME, materials science, CS, whatever.
Answer_with_writing_sample: Getting a job after majoring in bioengineering can be a challenge for several reasons, many of which stem from the nature of the field itself. Bioengineering is an interdisciplinary area that combines biology, engineering, and technology, which means candidates often need a diverse skill set. However, the job market tends to be saturated with applicants who may have similar qualifications, making it tough to stand out. Furthermore, many positions in bioengineering often require specific technical expertise or experience that cannot always be obtained during a typical undergraduate program. Internships and hands-on experience are crucial, yet not all universities offer robust opportunities for practical application. Networking is another essential aspect; many jobs are filled through connections rather than formal applications, and without a solid network, job seekers may find themselves at a disadvantage. Additionally, the evolving landscape of the industry—driven by rapid technological advancements—means that what was relevant in the past may not be applicable today. Employers often seek candidates who are not only knowledgeable but also adaptable and capable of continued learning. Finally, the path from academic training to employment can be hindered by the heavy focus on research in bioengineering programs, which may not align with the skills required for many industry roles. Consequently, while bioengineering is a promising field, the transition to employment is fraught with challenges that can complicate the job search for new graduates.
